title: Building, reading, and refusing to over-read a confidence interval

items.prompt: A large-sample analysis reports an estimate of the difference in next-morning fasting glucose of 7.5 mg/dL, with a standard error of 2.6 mg/dL, and specifies the normal approximation. Give the upper limit of its two-sided 95% confidence interval, in mg/dL, to one decimal place.
items.stimulus: Use the supplied normal-approximation multiplier of 1.96. Teaching example, not medical advice: this clinic and its numbers are invented.

answer.reasoning: The multiplier for a two-sided 95% interval is 1.96. The margin of error is 1.96 x 2.6 = 5.096 mg/dL, which rounds to 5.10. Adding it to the estimate gives 7.5 + 5.096 = 12.596, so the upper limit is 12.6 mg/dL. Subtracting it gives 2.4 mg/dL as the lower limit, so the interval is 2.4 to 12.6 and is 10.2 mg/dL wide. It excludes zero, and every value inside it is smaller than the upper limit of the original study's interval.
commonErrors: Answering 2.4, which is the lower limit rather than the upper one.
Answering 10.1 by using 1.0 times the standard error, or 5.1 by reporting the margin of error instead of the limit.
Using a multiplier other than the supplied 1.96, which changes the stated large-sample normal-approximation task.
Dividing by the square root of a sample size that was never given; the standard error has already been computed for you.

items.prompt: A trial reports a difference of 9.0 mg/dL with a 95% confidence interval of 0.7 to 17.3 mg/dL. Which statement about that interval is defensible?

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the true difference lies between 0.7 and 17.3 mg/dL.
If independent samples from the same defined population were repeatedly analysed with this adequate model, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true difference.
About 95% of patients in this population have a dinner-timing effect between 0.7 and 17.3 mg/dL.
If the study were repeated, there is a 95% probability the new estimate would fall between 0.7 and 17.3 mg/dL.
The true difference is 9.0 mg/dL, and 0.7 to 17.3 shows how accurately it was measured.

answer.summary: The statement about repeated studies and the proportion of intervals that would contain the true difference.
answer.reasoning: The confidence level is a conditional property of the procedure across repeated samples, so the defensible statement names the repeated sampling, the population, and the adequacy of the model. The probability statement about this interval treats the true difference as random when it is fixed and unknown; either this interval contains it or it does not. The statement about 95% of patients confuses an interval for a population average with the spread of individual people. The statement about a repeat estimate landing inside is a different quantity and is not what the level refers to. The last option asserts the true difference equals the point estimate, which a study does not establish. Even the defensible statement concerns random-error coverage under its assumptions; it does not repair bias or establish generalisability beyond the sampled population.
commonErrors: Choosing the probability statement, which is the dominant error and treats the fixed parameter as the random quantity.
Choosing the statement about patients, which reads an interval for an average as a reference range for individuals.
Choosing the statement about a repeat estimate, which swaps the parameter for a future observation.

items.prompt: A colleague writes: "We are 95% sure the true effect is somewhere between 0.7 and 17.3 mg/dL." In two or three sentences, name the quantity their sentence has treated as random, say why that quantity is fixed, and rewrite the sentence so it is defensible and conditional on the sampling and analysis model.

answer.correct: The true effect has been treated as random. It is a fixed unknown quantity belonging to the defined population, and it does not change when a sample is drawn; the interval is the thing that varies from sample to sample. A defensible rewrite: under the stated sampling and analysis model, the data are compatible with true effects from about 0.7 to about 17.3 mg/dL, and the procedure captures the true effect in about 95% of repeated samples when its conditions hold.
answer.summary: The true effect is the fixed quantity; the interval is what varies; the rewrite must not attach a probability to the parameter.
answer.reasoning: Two things could in principle vary: the parameter and the limits. Only the limits do. Recruiting sixty different people gives a different estimate, a different standard error, and a different pair of limits, while the true effect in that population is unchanged by who happened to be recruited. So a probability statement about whether a fixed number lies between two other fixed numbers has nothing left to be random. Any rewrite that either describes the long-run behaviour of the procedure, or states which parameter values the data are compatible with, is acceptable.
acceptableResponses: Names the true effect, the true difference, or the population parameter as the quantity wrongly treated as random.
Explains that the parameter is fixed and the interval varies across repeated samples.
Rewrites using the conditional long-run proportion of intervals that contain the true value.
Rewrites using compatibility under the stated model: the data are compatible with values from 0.7 to 17.3 mg/dL.
commonErrors: Saying the sentence is fine because 95% is only an approximation; the problem is the object of the probability, not its precision.
Rewriting as "we are 95% confident", which changes the wording and keeps the same claim.
Naming the sample or the sample size as the quantity treated as random, when both are known.
Rewriting into a statement about individual patients rather than the population parameter.

items.prompt: A large-sample trial with 150 patients in each arm reports a normal-approximation 95% confidence interval 12 units wide. The team wants an anticipated 95% interval 4 units wide, with the same outcome measure, population spread, design, and multiplier. How many patients per arm do they need?
items.stimulus: Teaching example, not medical advice: the trial is invented, and the question is about planning anticipated width only; a future realised interval will also depend on the new sample.

answer.reasoning: Width is twice the multiplier times the standard error, and the multiplier is unchanged because the level stays at 95%. So the width has to fall by the same factor as the standard error. Going from 12 units to 4 units is a factor of 3. The sample size sits under a square root in the standard error, so cutting the standard error by 3 needs 3 squared, which is 9, times as many patients: 150 x 9 = 1,350 per arm. The rule behind it is the same one the lesson used on the dinner-timing study, where four times the people bought half the width.
commonErrors: Answering 450 by scaling the sample size by 3 instead of by 3 squared, which forgets the square root.
Answering 600 by reasoning from the four-times-for-half-the-width rule without adjusting it to a factor of 3.
Answering 2,700 by applying the factor to the combined trial size instead of per arm.
Trying to change the confidence level to reach the target width, which would change what the interval claims.

items.prompt: A team has computed a two-sided 95% confidence interval. Which of the following changes would make the interval wider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reporting the interval at the 99% level instead of 95%.
Recruiting 100 patients per arm instead of 400.
Drawing from a population in which the outcome varies more between people.
Reporting the estimate and its limits to three decimal places instead of one.
Finding a larger point estimate, with the standard error unchanged.

answer.summary: Raising the level, recruiting fewer patients, and drawing from a more variable population.
answer.reasoning: Width is twice the multiplier times the standard error, so only those two quantities can move it. Raising the level to 99% raises the multiplier from 1.960 to 2.576 and widens the interval with no new data. Cutting the sample from 400 per arm to 100 is a factor of four, which doubles the standard error because the count sits under a square root. A more variable population raises the standard deviation that feeds the standard error. Reporting more decimal places changes nothing about the calculation; it only changes how the same numbers are printed. A larger point estimate slides the whole interval along the axis and leaves its width alone, which is exactly why an impressive estimate tells you nothing about how well the study pinned it down.
commonErrors: Selecting the larger point estimate, which moves the interval's centre without touching its width.
Selecting more decimal places, which confuses reporting precision with the precision of the estimate.
Selecting only the level change and missing that both inputs to the standard error also move the width.

items.prompt: Three trials report the difference in average fasting glucose as control minus intervention, in mg/dL, with a 95% confidence interval. Positive values mean the intervention group's average was lower; negative values mean it was higher. Trial P: 0.5 (0.2 to 0.8). Trial Q: 14.0 (-2.0 to 30.0). Trial R: 8.0 (5.0 to 11.0). For each trial say whether the interval excludes zero, identify the numerically tightest interval, and explain why Q is uninformative rather than evidence that the difference is zero.
items.stimulus: Teaching example, not medical advice: all three trials are invented. No clinical-importance threshold is supplied, so do not label an effect clinically small, large, beneficial, or harmful.

answer.correct: P and R exclude zero; Q does not. Trial P is numerically tightest, with width 0.6 mg/dL. Under the stated control-minus-intervention contrast, P and R are entirely positive, while Q remains compatible with negative, zero, and positive differences across a 32.0 mg/dL span. Q therefore has not located the parameter well; that absence of evidence is not evidence that the difference is zero. No clinical magnitude or value judgement follows because the item supplies no clinical threshold.
answer.summary: P and R exclude zero, Q does not; P is tightest, and Q's wide interval leaves direction and size unresolved rather than showing no difference.
answer.reasoning: Excluding zero is a question about location and is answered by looking at the limits: P runs 0.2 to 0.8 and R runs 5.0 to 11.0, both entirely positive under control minus intervention, while Q runs from -2.0 to 30.0 and straddles zero. Width answers the precision question: P is 0.6 wide, R is 6.0 wide, and Q is 32.0 wide. Q is compatible with values far from zero in both directions, so writing it up as no difference would convert an uninformative result into a negative one. Calling any compatible range clinically small or large would require a pre-stated threshold that this item does not provide.
acceptableResponses: States that P and R exclude zero and Q does not.
Identifies P as the numerically tightest interval and may note that R is ten times as wide.
Identifies Q as uninformative and explains that its interval covers negative, zero, and positive differences.
Distinguishes absence of evidence from evidence of absence, in any wording.
commonErrors: Writing that trial Q showed no effect, which is the error the item is built around.
Ranking the trials by the size of the point estimate, which puts Q first.
Calling any result clinically small, large, beneficial, or harmful without a stated threshold.
Saying trial R is best because it excludes zero by the widest margin, which confuses distance from zero with precision.

items.prompt: A diabetes service decides that it would only change its dietary advice if the true difference in next-morning fasting glucose were at least 6 mg/dL. The study in front of it reports 9.0 mg/dL with a 95% confidence interval of 0.7 to 17.3. Write a short paragraph for the meeting that states what the study does and does not settle against that threshold, and distinguishes the anticipated precision of a study four times the size from the unknown location of its realised interval. Do not recommend a change to anyone's care.
items.stimulus: Teaching example, not medical advice: the service, the study, and the 6 mg/dL threshold are invented for this item.

answer.correct: The interval excludes zero, so the study supports a positive direction under the stated contrast. It does not settle the service's question, because 6 mg/dL lies inside 0.7 to 17.3: the data remain compatible with a true difference below or above the threshold. With the same design and population spread, four times the people would be expected to cut the standard error from 4.13 to about 2.07 mg/dL and roughly halve the width. If the future estimate happened to remain 9.0, the interval would be about 4.9 to 13.1 and would still contain 6. That location is not predetermined: the future estimate and estimated spread are random, so the realised interval could shift. Whether 6 mg/dL is the right threshold is a clinical judgement, and no interval decides it.
answer.summary: Direction supported and threshold unsettled; four times the size approximately halves anticipated width, but 4.9 to 13.1 is conditional on the future estimate remaining 9.0, not a guaranteed future interval.
answer.reasoning: The threshold question is answered by asking where the chosen value sits relative to both limits, not only whether the interval excludes zero. Here 6 is between 0.7 and 17.3, so the study cannot choose between values below and above the threshold. The square-root rule says that, if design and population spread stay the same, four times the people approximately halves the anticipated standard error and width. Holding the estimate at 9.0 only for illustration gives about 4.9 to 13.1. A new sample will generate a new estimate and spread, so that conditional interval is useful for precision planning but is not a prediction of the realised limits. A complete answer preserves that distinction and keeps the threshold itself as a clinical choice.
acceptableResponses: States that the interval excludes zero and so supports the direction.
States that 6 mg/dL lies inside 0.7 to 17.3, so the threshold question is unsettled.
States that four times the sample approximately halves the anticipated standard error and interval width under unchanged design and spread.
Labels 4.9 to 13.1 mg/dL as conditional on the future estimate remaining 9.0, rather than a guaranteed future interval.
Notes that the conditional 4.9 to 13.1 interval would still contain 6 mg/dL.
Keeps the choice of threshold as a clinical judgement and makes no care recommendation.
commonErrors: Concluding that the service should change its advice because the estimate of 9.0 is above 6.
Treating the exclusion of zero as an answer to the threshold question.
Treating 4.9 to 13.1 as the predetermined interval from a future larger study.
Assuming a larger study would automatically resolve the threshold.
Reporting the larger study's interval as a quarter of the width instead of half, by scaling the width by the sample-size factor instead of its square root.

rubrics.title: Numerical work on interval limits and widths

criteria.description: The value is correct within the stated tolerance and is the quantity the item asked for, not a neighbouring one such as the other limit or the margin of error.
The answer carries the right units and is rounded as the item specified, with no silent change of scale.

rubrics.title: Selecting defensible statements about an interval

criteria.description: Every correct option is selected and no incorrect option is selected.

The response does not include an option that treats the fixed parameter as random, reads an interval for an average as a range for individuals, or confuses reporting precision with statistical precision.

rubrics.title: Written reading of a reported interval

criteria.description: States where the interval sits relative to the value it is being read against, whether that is zero or a stated threshold, and draws the right conclusion about direction.
Uses the width of the interval to say what range of effect sizes the study leaves open, including any arithmetic the item asked for.

Attaches no probability to the parameter, does not convert an uninformative interval into evidence of no effect, and keeps clinical judgement and care recommendations out of the statistical conclusion.
